title: Prostate Imaging -- Introduction
content: The prostate is a "walnut-shaped" gland located at the base of the bladder. It is part of the male reproductive system that produces and secretes a highly alkaline fluid into the seminal vesicles and the ejaculate. It contains glandular and stromal elements that are subject to enlargement and the development of adenocarcinoma in elderly patients. Infection is common in relatively younger patients. Imaging plays a vital role in the diagnosis of different prostatic pathologies, including early detection of carcinoma. Imaging also helps obtain tissue samples, measure prostatic size, identify intravesical extension, drain abscesses and post-procedure collections, and aid in staging and following malignancy.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Anatomy
content: The prostate is located in the pelvic cavity, inferior to the urinary bladder, surrounding the prostatic urethra. The gland comprises an apex resting on the urogenital diaphragm, a base attached to the bladder neck, and inferolateral surfaces resting on the levator ani fascia above the urogenital diaphragm. [1] See Image. Median Sagittal Section of Male Pelvis Anatomy.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Anatomy
content: Anatomically, it is divided into 2 lateral (right and left) and 1 median lobe. Histologically, it has a central zone (CZ) comprising 25% of the prostatic mass that forms the base; a peripheral zone (PZ) surrounding the central part, constituting 25% of the prostatic mass; and a transition zone (TZ) that surrounds the anterolateral portion of the urethra in a horseshoe-like fashion. [1] Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) typically occurs in the transition zone of the prostate. [1]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Anatomy
content: It is essential to know these histological zones because 75% of the adenocarcinomas arise from the peripheral zone, while 20% are from the transition zone. Only 10% of adenocarcinomas arise from the central zone. Prostatitis more often occurs in the central zone. Benign prostatic hyperplasia typically expands the transitional zone, resulting in the formation of an adenoma.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Anatomy
content: Sonographic evaluation can provide a general estimate of prostate size and contour, aiding in the assessment of prostatomegaly or bladder outlet obstruction. [2] While not as detailed as transrectal ultrasound, the transabdominal approach offers a non-invasive and accessible method to screen for prostate enlargement in symptomatic patients. [3] [4]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Anatomy
content: The prostate base is located at the bladder neck proximally and the membranous urethra inferiorly. An enlarged median lobe may extend into the bladder, causing an intravesical intrusion that is visible on ultrasound. [1] The pubic symphysis and dorsal vein complex are anterior, and the rectum is posterior. The pelvic side walls and levator ani are lateral, while the neurovascular bundles and primary arterial supply are posterolateral. [1] The seminal vesicles are paired hypoechoic sacs adjacent to the posterior prostatic base. [5]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Anatomy
content: In male patients, the prostate gland may be partially visualized transabdominally, particularly when the bladder is full. The prostate is located just inferior to the bladder and posterior to the pubic symphysis. [4] Sonographic evaluation can provide a general estimate of prostate size and contour, aiding in the assessment of prostatomegaly or bladder outlet obstruction. While not as detailed as transrectal ultrasound, the transabdominal approach offers a non-invasive and accessible method to screen for prostate enlargement in symptomatic patients and estimate the prostate's volume. [3] [4]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Plain Films
content: Plain radiographs have limited prostate evaluation utility but are rarely used as part of a skeletal survey to assess or follow metastases. Other imaging modalities like bone scans are used for assessing bone metastases, and computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis has been used to stage prostate cancer, although this is being rapidly replaced by PSMA/PET scans, which are more sensitive. [6] Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the prostate is sensitive and specific for identifying possible prostate malignancies, local extension, and regional lymph node involvement. [7]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Computed Tomography
content: The CT scan does not sufficiently define detailed prostate anatomy or pathology. It may show a hyperdense central zone with density adjusted to around 40 to 60 Hounsfield Units (HU), and the peripheral zone may appear hypodense, with density between 10 and 25 HU. [8] Focal peripheral zone lesions with >25 HU on CT might be suspicious for prostatic malignancy. [9]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Computed Tomography -- Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
content: CT scans are not typically used to diagnose benign prostatic hyperplasia, but BPH can be identified when the prostate extends above the pubic symphysis on axial imaging. BPH can also be diagnosed on a CT scan with a volume greater than 30 mL (measured using coronal reformatted images).

title: Prostate Imaging -- Computed Tomography -- Prostatitis (Inflammation)
content: In prostatitis, the gland appears diffusely hypodense with symmetric or asymmetric enlargement. Prostatic abscesses are well-defined hypoattenuating (approximately fluid density, around -19 to 13 HU) areas with peripheral rim enhancement. The progression of the disease can be monitored with a CT scan or sonography. [10]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Computed Tomography -- Prostate Cancer
content: Prostatic malignancy appears as contrast-enhancing areas, particularly in the venous phase of the imaging study. These areas can be focal or diffuse and are found most often within the peripheral zone. CT scans play a role in imaging carcinomas to assess local and distant spread; however, PSMA/PET scans are far more sensitive and are rapidly replacing CT scans for staging purposes. [11]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Magnetic Resonance
content: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an excellent modality for prostate imaging due to its better contrast resolution and superior ability to detect malignant intraprostatic nodules. [12] MRI can differentiate anatomical zones and detect any abnormalities. Prostate MRI is performed with a pelvic coil and is sensitive in detecting malignancy and assessing its local extension. The use of an endorectal coil provides even more detailed imaging information and better resolution (see Image. Normal Prostate, Magnetic Resonance Image Using Endorectal Coil). With recent advances like multiparametric MRI (mp-MRI), functional MRI, and MRI-guided fusion biopsies, MRI is increasingly useful in detecting low-grade and low-volume prostate carcinoma.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Magnetic Resonance
content: Necessary MRI sequences include T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with an apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map, and dynamic intravenous contrast-enhanced imaging. DWI analyzes the diffusion of water molecules at the cellular level. ADC is a qualitative measure of average water diffusion per voxel. DWI is particularly important in the diagnosis of prostate carcinoma and prostatitis, including abscesses. [13]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Magnetic Resonance -- Normal Anatomy
content: The peripheral zone appears homogeneously hyperintense on T2WI, with a hypointense capsule. The transition zone exhibits heterogeneity, whereas the seminal vesicles appear uniformly hyperintense on T2WI.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Magnetic Resonance -- Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)
content: MRI delineates zonal anatomy, its elements, and gland volume as well as zonal volume. BPH appears as a heterogeneous TZ on T2WI. Due to glandular or stromal tissue enlargement, enlarged nodules in BPH show increased or decreased signals on T2WI. Glandular enlargement appears as bright signals on T2WI, while fibromuscular and stromal elements are dark on T2WI. Estimation of the stromal and glandular ratio helps to choose appropriate medical therapy. [14] Stromal enlargement may mimic transitional zone cancer due to low intensity on T2WI, diffusion restriction, and contrast enhancement, similar to prostatic carcinoma. Stromal hyperplasia can be differentiated by having a more well-defined and encapsulated appearance. [15] On MRI, BPH can be divided into 7 types. [14]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Magnetic Resonance -- Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)
content: Type 0 = Prostate is no larger than 25 cc with little or no zonal enlargement. Type 1 = Bilateral enlargement of the transition zone. Type 2 = Retrourethral enlargement. Type 3 = Retrourethral and bilateral transition zone enlargement. Type 4 = Pedunculated enlargement (multiple or solitary). Type 5 = Pedunculated with bilateral transition zone and/or retrourethral enlargement. Type 6 = Subtrigonal or ectopic enlargement. Type  7= Other combinations of enlargements.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Magnetic Resonance -- Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)
content: Besides diagnosing BPH, MRI plays an important role in identifying carcinoma when a patient with BPH has a confirmed increased PSA level and is suspicious or at high risk for developing prostate cancer. [14]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Magnetic Resonance -- Prostatitis
content: Bacterial prostatitis is acute or chronic and is more common in the peripheral zone. Acute prostatitis appears T2 hyperintense with increased contrast enhancement. Chronic prostatitis is typically hypointense on T2WI and exhibits poor contrast enhancement. Chronic prostatitis demonstrates increased diffuse restriction due to inflammatory cell infiltrate. These findings mimic prostatic carcinoma. However, the degree of diffusion restriction is lower than that of carcinoma. Non-necrotic granulomatous prostatitis also appears hypointense on T2WI, with diffusion restriction; however, unlike chronic prostatitis, there is no enhancement on post-contrast imaging.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Magnetic Resonance -- Prostatitis
content: The necrotic area of granulomatous prostatitis exhibits an increased signal on T2WI. In patients with extraprostatic extension of the granulomas, it's challenging to differentiate them from carcinomas. [15] [16] Prostatitis may progress into abscesses, which appear hyperintense on T2WI, hypointense on T1-weighted images, and exhibit peripheral contrast enhancement. Prostatic abscesses show restricted diffusion and low ADC values. [17]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Magnetic Resonance -- Prostate Cancer
content: Prostate carcinoma is associated with high worldwide morbidity and mortality. MRI, especially mp-MRI, is useful for cancer detection and helps to identify suspicious lesions for biopsy. MRI-fusion guided prostate biopsies have proven to be far superior to transrectal ultrasound-guided (TRUS) biopsies. [18] [19] [20] [21] Pre-biopsy MRIs help avoid over-staging errors, which may occur due to biopsy artifacts, and understaging due to otherwise unrecognized seminal vesicle or lymph node involvement, as well as identifying extraprostatic tumor extensions and regional lymph node involvement. [22] MRI also detects anterior, lateral, and apex lesions, which may be missed by standard transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsies without MRI fusion guidance.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Magnetic Resonance -- Prostate Cancer
content: The malignant lesions are typically located in the peripheral zone, exhibiting T2WI hypointensity, focal enhancement, and low diffusivity. Ill-defined and T2 hypointense lesions in the periphery are highly suspicious for carcinoma. Though malignancy is less common in the transition zone and elsewhere, non-circumscribed, spiculated, relatively T2 hypointense lesions are considered suspicious for prostatic malignancy regardless of location within the gland.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Magnetic Resonance -- Prostate Cancer
content: PI-RADS 1: Cancer risk is Highly Unlikely: normal T2WI and diffusion-weighted imaging(DWI)/ADC. PI-RADS 2: Cancer risk is Unlikely: May have a circumscribed lesion. Heterogeneity on T2WI and hypointensity PZ on DW/ADC (see Image. Magnetic Resonance Image of Prostate, Imaging Reporting and Data System-2 Classification) PI-RADS 3: Cancer risk is Equivocal: Heterogenous lesion with obscured margin on T2WI: hyperintense on DWI and hypointense on ADC.(see Image. Magnetic Resonance Image of Prostate, Imaging Reporting and Data System 3 Classification) PI-RADS 4: Cancer risk is Likely: Non-circumscribed lesion up to 1.5 cm, moderately homogenously hypointense on T2WI; hyperintensity on DWI and hypointense on ADC. PI-RADS 5: Cancer risk is Highly Likely: Similar to PI-RADS 4, but lesion is >1.5 cm and/or evidence of extraprostatic extension.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Ultrasonography
content: Ultrasound is widely available for prostate evaluation, but also for performing guided prostatic biopsy. Transabdominal (TAUS) or transrectal sonography can be used to evaluate the prostate, and transrectal is preferred for biopsy. See Image. Transrectal Ultrasound Guided Biopsy of the Prostate. The prostate is examined with TAUS by a transducer placed just above the pubic symphysis, with a fluid-filled urinary bladder serving as an acoustic window. The average normal measurements are 3.75 to 4.00 × 2.5 to 3.00 × 3.1 to 3.8 cm (width × height × length) with a volume of 20 to 25 cc. The prostate volume is calculated using the formula for measuring any ellipsoidal structure, which is 0.5236 × height (H) × width (W) × length (L). [24]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Ultrasonography
content: Transabdominal ultrasonography is limited in obese patients and those with significant ascites, as bladder filling is not sufficient to reliably evaluate prostate volume. If necessary, transrectal ultrasonography can be performed in such cases. TRUS is also necessary for suspected prostatic pathology during the clinical exam, persistently increased serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, prostatic inflammation or abscess, and follow-up of prostatic cancer, as transrectal ultrasonography allows detailed evaluation of the prostate.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Ultrasonography
content: For TRUS, an endorectal transducer having a frequency of 8 to 10 MHz is delicately inserted into the rectum. Prostate volume is measured similarly to TRAS by obtaining width, height, and length. The gland is evaluated for its shape, symmetry, echogenicity, and integrity of the prostatic capsule. Periprostatic structures, e.g., seminal vesicles, neurovascular bundles, and blood vessels, are assessed for any abnormality, especially in suspected prostate carcinoma. [25] Elastography is a vital aid performed during transrectal ultrasounds to evaluate the firmness of the prostate tissue. Areas of increased firmness are often identified on elastography and are considered suspicious for malignancy, which may not show any abnormal echogenicity on grayscale prostatic imaging.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Ultrasonography
content: The prostate is generally divided into anatomic zones: the peripheral, central, transitional, and periurethral zones. [1] It also contains an anterior fibromuscular stroma, which is composed of non-glandular tissue. [1] The peripheral zone is where most prostate cancers are found and comprises about 70% of the total mass of the prostate. [2] Prostate cancer is unique in that it is typically multifocal, whereas most other malignancies tend to be unifocal unless they have metastasized. [12] The central zone contains glandular tissue, where the ejaculatory ducts travel to empty into the posterior prostatic urethra. [1] It is the most common area affected by prostatitis. [26] The transitional zone is the smallest component and surrounds the urethra. It is the primary site of benign prostatic hyperplasia. [1]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Ultrasonography -- Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
content: TAS OR TRUS assesses the prostate volume to determine the course of management, ie, prostatic volume more than 80 cm 3 qualifies for open surgery or HoLEP laser prostatectomy; otherwise, transurethral resection or 1 of the newer minimally invasive BPH therapies (Aquablation, laser transurethral ablation, prostatic urethral lift (Urolift), water infusion theramal therapy, and similar) are chosen for surgical management in patients who have failed or do not want drug therapy. [2] The European Association of Urology (EAU) suggests measuring prostatic volume via TRUS and residual urinary bladder post-void urine volume through TAUS. Abdominal ultrasound examinations should be supplemented by visualization of the upper urinary tract to assess the degree of urinary tract dilatation, and should also examine the adrenal glands. [27]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Ultrasonography -- Prostate Cancer
content: Prostatic malignancy is difficult to diagnose with ultrasonography alone, as the tumor is often isoechoic to the surrounding normal gland, although it generally tends to be somewhat hypoechoic. [28] Transrectal ultrasonography with color Doppler or power Doppler can identify angiogenesis, showing dilated and tortuous vessels, but it cannot detect small tumor foci. The overall diagnostic value of ultrasound is around 30% to 40%. [25] Therefore, it's mainly used as a guide for prostatic biopsies. [28] It is proven to improve cancer detection, especially in men who have a positive PSA and high PSA density (PSA/prostate volume in cc >0.15). [29] Ultrasound (US) may help identify local tumor spread for staging purposes; however, this is more reliably done with prostate MRI.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Ultrasonography -- Prostate Cancer
content: Some advances, such as elastography, identify consistency differences and aid in tumor diagnosis and guided biopsy. On elastography, the consistency of a neoplasm appears firmer than that of the surrounding normal tissue. 3-dimensional TRUS enables computer processing of sectional images of the prostate, providing more detailed information about its morphology, surrounding structures, and other features. [25] The contrast-enhanced US has a high sensitivity to differentiate neoplasm from normal prostate tissue and is more useful for US-guided biopsies. [30] Prostate cancer is unique in that it is usually a multifocal lesion, while most other malignancies are unifocal. [12]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Ultrasonography -- Prostatitis and Prostatic Abscesses
content: Prostatitis is usually a clinical diagnosis. [26] Sonography in prostatitis frequently demonstrates an enlarged and/or deformed gland with inhomogeneous echotexture. [31] Acute prostatitis may result in a parenchymal abscess, which appears as a hypoechoic or fluid-consistency lesion within the prostate parenchyma. Ultrasound is performed not only for diagnosis but also for planning to evacuate it under transrectal ultrasound guidance. [32] Ultrasound is useful in intraprostatic antibiotic injections in chronic prostatitis when pain is exacerbating. [33]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Nuclear Medicine
content: Nuclear medicine plays a role in the diagnosis, staging/re-staging, and therapy of prostate carcinoma. Skeletal metastases can be identified with a bone scan. Positron emission tomography (PET) is a diagnostic imaging technique that assesses the activity and spread of malignant tumors throughout the body. In particular, the choline derivative radiotracer 18F-fluorocholine (F-FCH) is currently used as a tracer for diagnosing prostate carcinoma. PET, when combined with CT (PET/CT) and MRI (PET/MRI), adds metabolic/functional data derived from PET to CT or MRI findings. [34] [35]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Nuclear Medicine
content: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is expressed on the cell surface of carcinoma, nodal metastasis, and metastases to the bones. Ga-labeled PSMA inhibitors are widely used PET tracers and are now gaining popularity, not only for diagnosis but also for therapy when PSMA antigens are merged with radiotherapeutic elements. [35]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Nuclear Medicine
content: PSMA/PET scans can be used for patients with PSA levels as low as 0.2 ng/mL; however, their sensitivity increases as the PSA level rises. At a PSA of 0.5, a PSMA/PET scan has a 50% chance of picking up a 5 mm lesion. [36] [37]

title: Prostate Imaging -- Angiography
content: Angiography can be utilized for prostatic artery embolization in patients with BPH and bleeding. It is an interventional technique for managing patients with lower urinary tract symptoms secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia. Prostatic artery embolization improves lower urinary tract symptoms and can be used to treat otherwise intractable bleeding.

title: Prostate Imaging -- Clinical Significance
content: Prostate imaging plays a vital role in identifying various pathologies, including infection, enlargement, and carcinoma. It is crucial in staging the carcinoma. PI-RADS is a standardized classification based on MRI findings, which helps in further management. US or MRI-guided procedures are also widely used for both diagnosis and therapy.
